title: Fio Corporation Implied Undertakings Motion (2014 TCC)
subject: Implied Undertakings Motion: Use of Discovery Documents to Reassess
summary: In Fio Corporation v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 58, an SR&ED implied undertakings motion, the Tax Court of Canada held the Minister bound, like all litigants, to seek leave before using discovery documents to reassess. The Federal Court of Appeal set the order aside because the documents were already disclosed to CRA auditors before the appeal.
metaDescription: Analyze the February 2014 Tax Court of Canada decision for Fio Corporation concerning an implied undertakings motion in SR&ED.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background

The interlocutory decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Fio Corporation v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 58 (2014 DTC 1021), handed down on February 20, 2014, together with its subsequent appellate review by the Federal Court of Appeal in Canada v. Fio Corporation, 2015 FCA 236 (478 N.R. 194, [2016] 2 C.T.C. 1), represents a watershed precedent in Canadian tax litigation. Arising within the context of a Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax dispute, the ruling addresses a critical tension in Canadian tax administration: the boundary between the statutory audit and reassessment powers of the Minister of National Revenue (the Minister) under the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the ITA), and the common law implied undertaking rule governing documentary and oral discovery in judicial proceedings before the Tax Court of Canada.
The Taxpayer's Profile and Underlying Claim

The Appellant, Fio Corporation, is a Canadian biotechnology and medical diagnostics enterprise engaged in the research, design, and development of integrated biosensor systems, genomic DNA pathogen detection arrays, and automated mobile in vitro diagnostic devices, most notably the Deki Reader utilized for interpreting rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) in clinical field evaluations. In conducting these technological development activities, the taxpayer claimed SR&ED expenditure deductions under section 37 of the ITA and corresponding Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under section 127 of the ITA across multiple taxation years, including its 2007 and 2008 taxation years.

Following an administrative audit and technical review by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), during which a CRA science auditor and financial auditor attended Fio Corporation's offices in October 2009 and were given access to its documents, the Minister issued Notices of Reassessment dated March 2, 2011 and March 11, 2011 disallowing a portion of the amounts claimed as eligible SR&ED expenditures for the 2007 and 2008 taxation years. After serving Notices of Objection, and without having received a response from the Minister to those objections, Fio Corporation instituted formal litigation on April 12, 2012 by filing a Notice of Appeal with the Tax Court of Canada under the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure), SOR/90-688a (the General Procedure Rules). In a proactive effort to expedite the resolution of the dispute, on the same day it filed its Notice of Appeal, Fio Corporation delivered to the Respondent's counsel at the Department of Justice, acting for the Attorney General of Canada (AGC), a package comprising a copy of the Notice of Appeal, its list of documents (partial disclosure) under Rule 81, seven binders containing the 260 documents noted in that list, a Request to Admit, and an annotated Request to Admit. In an accompanying cover letter, counsel for Fio Corporation stated that the package had been prepared with the goal of minimizing time and cost in resolving the appeal, and asked that a meeting be arranged as quickly as possible with a CRA officer able to instruct Department of Justice counsel, in the hope of reaching a settlement of the appeal of the 2007 and 2008 reassessments.
The Tax Authority's Challenge and Collateral Reassessment

Rather than confining the use of the disclosed documentation to the litigation or settlement of the 2007 and 2008 appeals before the Tax Court, the Department of Justice forwarded the documents to the Minister, whose CRA officials reviewed them. Relying at least in part on documents included in Fio Corporation's list of documents, the Minister issued further Notices of Reassessment in October 2012 (the Second Reassessments), which reassessed the same 2007 and 2008 taxation years already under appeal to further reduce the SR&ED claims, together with a consequential adjustment to the 2009 taxation year.

In response to the Crown's collateral use of its settlement and discovery disclosures, Fio Corporation brought an interlocutory motion before the Tax Court of Canada seeking severe sanctions against the Minister and the AGC. Specifically, the taxpayer moved for an order vacating the October 2012 reassessments of its 2007, 2008 and 2009 taxation years, directing the Minister and/or the AGC to pay $100,000 to Fio Corporation as punishment for contempt of the Tax Court of Canada, and awarding Fio Corporation the costs of the motion on a full indemnity basis, on the ground that making the reassessments violated the implied undertaking rule.

In defending the use of the documents, the Minister advanced several legal arguments, which were summarized at paragraphs 24 to 30 of the Tax Court's reasons. First, as the centrepiece of her argument, the Minister contended that, because of her duty under the ITA to assess and the taxpayer's statutory obligations to keep and produce records, her relationship with the taxpayer differs from that of "normal litigants", so that, while the implied undertaking rule may apply to her in certain situations, it does not apply where she uses information provided in discovery to reassess the same taxpayer with respect to the same issue and the same taxation year. Second, the Minister argued pre-emption by section 241 of the ITA, asserting that the statutory provision regulating the confidentiality and permissible disclosure of "taxpayer information" by Crown officials operates as a comprehensive "complete code" that ousts and supersedes the common law implied undertaking rule. Third, the Minister raised a preliminary issue, arguing that the implied undertaking rule did not apply because Fio Corporation had voluntarily provided the documents on April 12, 2012, before, in her view, its appeal had commenced (she contended that it commenced only when the Court served the Notice of Appeal on May 7, 2012); she also relied on the Court's partial disclosure regime and on the taxpayer's low expectation of privacy in its tax records, and alternatively asked for an opportunity to seek relief if a breach were found. The reasons do not record the Minister arguing that the Tax Court of Canada, as a statutory court created under the Tax Court of Canada Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. T-2, lacked jurisdiction to vacate a reassessment as a remedy for breach of an undertaking; the Court addressed its remedial jurisdiction in response to Fio Corporation's request that the Second Reassessments be vacated.
Governing Statutory and Common Law Framework

The dispute in Fio Corporation sits at the intersection of Canadian statutory tax law, procedural rules of court, and Supreme Court of Canada common law jurisprudence. The primary doctrinal pillar is the common law implied undertaking rule, articulated authoritatively by the Supreme Court of Canada in Juman v. Doucette, 2008 SCC 8, and Lac d'Amiante du Québec Ltée v. 2858-0702 Québec Inc., 2001 SCC 51. This doctrine mandates that all documentary and oral information obtained by a party through the compulsion of pre-trial discovery is subject to an implied undertaking to the court that the information will not be used for any collateral or ulterior purpose outside the specific litigation in which it was disclosed, absent the consent of the producing party or prior leave of the court.

Interacting with this common law doctrine is section 241 of the ITA. Subsection 241(1) prohibits Crown officials from knowingly providing, allowing access to, or using "taxpayer information" except as authorized by specific statutory exceptions, such as subsection 241(3), which permits disclosure in legal proceedings relating to the administration or enforcement of the ITA, and subsection 241(4), which permits internal use by officials in the administration and enforcement of the ITA. Simultaneously, the remedial powers of the Court are framed by section 171 of the ITA and sections 12 and 13 of the Tax Court of Canada Act. While section 171 of the ITA enumerates the statutory ways in which the Tax Court may dispose of an appeal from an assessment—namely dismissing it, or allowing it and vacating, varying, or referring the assessment back to the Minister—the Tax Court in Fio held that, as both a superior court and a statutory court, it possesses, applying the Supreme Court of Canada's reasoning in R. v. Cunningham, 2010 SCC 10, an implied jurisdiction by necessary implication to control its own process and ensure its proper functioning as a court of law, which complements Rule 4 of the General Procedure Rules, under which the rules are to be liberally construed to secure the just, most expeditious, and least expensive determination of every proceeding on its merits. Finally, underlying the documentary production in SR&ED appeals is the substantive statutory framework of sections 37 and 127 and subsection 248(1) of the ITA, which place the burden on the taxpayer to establish that claimed activities satisfy the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1), that expenditures qualify under section 37, and that ITCs calculated under section 127 are properly reduced by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments.
The Court's Final Holding and Appellate Trajectory

In Fio Corporation v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 58, the Tax Court of Canada emphatically rejected the Minister's assertion of special status. At paragraph 48 of the ruling, the Court stated that it could not accept an argument that provides more favourable treatment to one of the parties appearing before the Court, concluding at paragraph 50 that the Respondent Minister, like all litigants, is bound by the implied undertaking rule. The Court further held that, if the Minister considered that her duty to assess or a provision such as section 241 of the ITA overrode the implied undertaking rule, she should have applied to the Court for leave before the CRA used the documents to reassess, since leave is never granted automatically; in comments it described as not needed for its decision, the Court added that section 241 is an administrative confidentiality provision whose subsection 241(4) merely provides exceptions to the prohibition in subsection 241(1) and does not override common law rules such as the implied undertaking rule.

Finding that the Minister's unilateral use of the disclosed documents to reassess Fio Corporation constituted a breach of the implied undertaking and an abuse of process, the Tax Court affirmed its implied jurisdiction to control its own process, holding that statutory limits on its jurisdiction when disposing of an appeal of an assessment do not apply in respect of a breach of an implied undertaking, so that the Court may vacate an assessment if it considers that the appropriate remedy for a breach of an undertaking to the Court. Because it was not clear from the affidavit evidence that the documents were the only information supporting the Second Reassessments, the Tax Court declined to vacate them; it also held that contempt was not an appropriate remedy, refusing the requested $100,000 payment, and refused costs on a full indemnity (solicitor and client) basis, which it reserved for reprehensible, outrageous or scandalous behaviour. Instead, its order dated February 20, 2014 (i) prohibited the Respondent from using any documents obtained in the course of discovery in the appeal instituted on April 12, 2012 in any other proceeding before the Tax Court or any other court, excluding documents the CRA had obtained before the appeal was instituted, so that the Minister would have to defend any appeal of the Second Reassessments without those documents; (ii) awarded Fio Corporation substantial costs of $25,000 in light of the Respondent's conduct, which the Court found to be an abuse of process that was not inadvertent; and (iii) gave the Respondent 30 days to apply to the Court for leave to use the documents in another proceeding.

Subsequently, in Canada v. Fio Corporation, 2015 FCA 236, decided on October 30, 2015, the Federal Court of Appeal allowed the Crown's appeal from 2014 TCC 58, noting at paragraph 12 that the implied undertaking rule is not found in the General Procedure Rules but that it was not disputed that the rule applies to litigants before the Tax Court of Canada. The Federal Court of Appeal held that the Tax Court Judge had made a palpable and overriding error in finding that the documents were first disclosed to the Minister in April 2012: the evidence of Fio Corporation's own affiant, which Fio Corporation did not dispute on appeal, was that all of the Discovery Documents had already been made available to the CRA's science and financial auditors in 2009 and 2010, before the appeal commenced. Because the implied undertaking rule does not apply to evidence disclosed before the Tax Court proceedings commence, or to evidence a party was not compelled to produce in those proceedings, it did not apply to the Discovery Documents; the Court expressly declined to decide whether documents listed under Rule 81 are compelled or whether the October 2012 reassessments gave rise to new litigation, stated that nothing in its reasons endorsed the Tax Court's conclusions on those questions, set aside the Tax Court's order (including the $25,000 costs award), and dismissed Fio Corporation's motion with costs. Together, 2014 TCC 58 and 2015 FCA 236 establish the definitive legal framework governing documentary disclosure, Crown conduct, and multi-year evidentiary risk in Canadian SR&ED disputes.
2. Core Legal, Procedural, and Evidentiary Failures

A comprehensive examination of Fio Corporation reveals two interlocking tiers of legal and evidentiary failure: first, the procedural failures committed by both the Crown and the taxpayer regarding the timing, compulsion, and protection of litigation disclosures, including the fact that the documents had already been made available to CRA auditors before the appeal began; and second, the substantive SR&ED technical, contractual, and documentation deficiencies, which neither decision addresses, that can allow documentary production in one appeal to support further CRA reassessments, whether of the years under appeal, as occurred in Fio, or of adjacent taxation years.
Procedural and Statutory Failures in Discovery Governance
The Crown's Misapplication of Section 241 and Unilateral Self-Help

The primary legal failure penalized by the Tax Court in 2014 TCC 58 was the Minister's conflation of administrative statutory powers with judicial discovery rights. Under sections 231.1 and 231.2 of the ITA, the CRA enjoys broad administrative audit powers to inspect books and records and issue Requirements for Information (RFIs). Furthermore, under subsection 241(4) of the ITA, CRA officials are statutorily permitted to share taxpayer information internally for the administration and enforcement of the ITA. Counsel for the Minister argued before the Tax Court that section 241 of the ITA was a complete code governing the use of taxpayer information that, in effect, overrode the implied undertaking rule, so that the CRA could use documents obtained in the appeal to reassess the same 2007 and 2008 taxation years already under appeal.

As the Tax Court stated in 2014 TCC 58, in comments it described as not needed for its decision, section 241 is an administrative provision intended to protect the confidentiality of taxpayer information, and subsection 241(4) merely provides exceptions to the prohibition in subsection 241(1); it does not override common law rules such as the implied undertaking rule. Once a tax dispute enters the Tax Court of Canada, the Minister steps into the shoes of a litigant subject to the Court's rules and common law doctrines. The rationale of the implied undertaking rule, as established in Juman v. Doucette, 2008 SCC 8, is rooted in the protection of privacy and the promotion of candid, exhaustive disclosure during discovery. Because, as the Tax Court reasoned, parties proceeding under either the partial disclosure (Rule 81) or full disclosure (Rule 82) rules are required to disclose documents adverse to their interests (an appellant under partial disclosure being required by Rule 105 to produce on request any document in its possession or control), even where such disclosures invade corporate privacy or reveal sensitive scientific and commercial secrets, the court imposes a shield prohibiting the recipient from using compelled information for any purpose other than the proceeding in which it was compelled, although the Federal Court of Appeal in 2015 FCA 236 expressly left open whether documents listed under Rule 81 are compelled. Because the Respondent used the documents to reassess without first applying for leave to vary the undertaking under the Juman test (under which the applicant must demonstrate a superior public interest in disclosure, and an undertaking is set aside only in exceptional circumstances), the Tax Court held that the Crown had committed an abuse of process that was not inadvertent, although the Federal Court of Appeal later set aside the order on the ground that the rule did not apply to documents already made available to the CRA during the audit.
The Taxpayer's Procedural Trap: Voluntary Pre-Discovery Disclosure Versus Compelled Production

While 2014 TCC 58 censured the Minister's conduct, the appellate ruling in Canada v. Fio Corporation, 2015 FCA 236, turned on a decisive factual weakness in the taxpayer's position: the documents it sought to protect had already been made available to the CRA's science and financial auditors in 2009 and 2010, before the appeal commenced. In Canadian SR&ED disputes, taxpayers frequently experience severe working capital constraints when refundable ITCs are withheld during prolonged CRA audits and objections. Consequently, upon filing a Notice of Appeal, taxpayers and their advisors are often tempted to immediately hand over supplementary technical reports, lab notebooks, clinical trial results, and financial reconciliations to the Department of Justice with a cover letter requesting an early settlement, much as Fio Corporation, on the day it filed its Notice of Appeal, delivered to Department of Justice counsel its Rule 81 list of documents, seven binders containing the 260 listed documents, and a Request to Admit, under a cover letter seeking an early settlement meeting.

The legal failure in this approach lies in the strict prerequisite of compulsion under Canadian common law. Unlike certain provincial civil procedure codes that codify a "deemed undertaking" rule with specific statutory triggers, the implied undertaking rule in the Tax Court of Canada, which is not codified in the General Procedure Rules, applies only to evidence a party is compelled to disclose in the course of the litigation; examinations for discovery and court-ordered production are clear examples, whereas the Federal Court of Appeal in 2015 FCA 236 expressly left open whether documents listed under Rule 81 (partial disclosure) are compelled, after the Tax Court had found that Fio Corporation's Rule 81 documents were provided pursuant to the Court's discovery rules. As the Federal Court of Appeal clarified in 2015 FCA 236, the implied undertaking rule does not apply to any evidence disclosed before the commencement of the Tax Court proceedings, such as documents made available to CRA auditors during an administrative audit, or to any evidence a party produced in those proceedings but was not compelled to produce. Neither decision treated Fio Corporation's cover letter, which stated that the package had been prepared with the goal of minimizing time and cost in resolving the appeal and sought an early settlement meeting, as creating any protection; such a letter may invoke settlement privilege regarding the admissibility of concessions, but it does not insulate underlying pre-existing facts or documents from audit use or create a court-enforced implied undertaking. Because all of the documents had already been made available to CRA auditors during the 2009 and 2010 audit, no implied undertaking ever attached to them, and Fio Corporation had not sought a Protective and Confidentiality Order from the Tax Court; as a result, the Minister was free to rely on them, in particular the four documents on which the October 2012 reassessments were based, to reassess the same 2007 and 2008 taxation years under appeal, with a consequential adjustment to 2009.
Substantive SR&ED Legal, Technical, and Documentation Deficiencies Triggering Multi-Year Spillover

In Canadian SR&ED practice, the procedural dispute in Fio Corporation does not occur in a vacuum. Understanding why the documents in Fio Corporation's list of documents prompted the CRA to reassess the 2007 and 2008 taxation years under appeal (with a consequential 2009 adjustment), and how similar productions could expose other taxation years, requires analyzing the substantive vulnerabilities embedded in multi-year R&D documentation. When a biotechnology or medical hardware enterprise submits bulk project records to substantiate historical SR&ED claims, four recurring substantive deficiencies in those records routinely provide the CRA with the evidentiary basis to disqualify claims or claw back ITCs in subsequent fiscal periods.
Failure to Demarcate Technological Uncertainty from Subsequent Routine Engineering and Clinical Field Validation

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA and the governing five-question jurisprudential test established by the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, a claimant must prove the existence of a "technological uncertainty"—a technological obstacle or capability gap that cannot be resolved using standard practice, routine engineering, or publicly available scientific knowledge.

In the medical diagnostics and biosensor sector, exemplified by Fio Corporation's development of DNA pathogen sensors and the Deki Reader mobile diagnostic platform, R&D projects naturally span multiple fiscal years. In early taxation years such as 2007 and 2008, work typically focuses on core technological uncertainties: resolving optical reflectance anomalies across varying ambient lighting conditions, engineering microfluidic blood glucose or pathogen hybridization arrays, or developing proprietary image-processing algorithms. However, in subsequent taxation years, activities frequently transition into clinical field evaluations, user-interface localization, regulatory type-approval compliance (such as electromagnetic compatibility and specific absorption rate standards), and validation studies in foreign jurisdictions. When a taxpayer submits longitudinal project summaries or post-2008 clinical validation publications—such as field evaluation reports demonstrating that the device successfully met clinical performance objectives in Tanzania or Colombia—to prove that its 2007–2008 work eventually succeeded, CRA Research and Technology Advisors scrutinize the timeline in those documents to conclude that technological uncertainty had already been resolved by the end of 2008. The CRA then uses those exact documents to reassess post-2008 taxation years, disqualifying later expenditures as routine product validation, beta testing, or commercial deployment rather than eligible experimental development under paragraph (c) of the subsection 248(1) SR&ED definition.
Lack of a Structured, Year-Segregated Process of Systematic Investigation

Canadian jurisprudence consistently holds that technological advancement cannot be claimed merely by pointing to an innovative end-product; the taxpayer must demonstrate a systematic investigation or search carried out by means of experiment or analysis (CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393). A pervasive documentation failure occurs when taxpayers prepare retrospective "settlement binders" that aggregate multi-year engineering efforts into a single continuous narrative without isolating specific hypotheses formulated, experimental protocols executed, and analytical conclusions reached within each discrete 12-month taxation year. When such unsegregated records are handed over in an appeal, they often reveal that the experimental iterations actually occurred in a different fiscal period than claimed, or that work in an adjacent taxation year consisted of trial-and-error debugging lacking formulated scientific hypotheses, prompting immediate cross-year reassessments.
Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation and Unsegregated Financial Costing

To qualify for deductions under subsection 37(1) and ITCs under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, expenditures must be directly attributable to, or under the proxy method directly engaged in, the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Furthermore, section 37 requires strict territorial and functional cut-offs: foreign field trials or clinical evaluations conducted outside Canada, such as field evaluations in Colombia or Tanzania, are severely restricted, with salary or wages for SR&ED carried on outside Canada deductible only within subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), which cap them at 10% of the salary or wages for SR&ED carried on in Canada. When a taxpayer discloses unredacted general ledgers, multi-year vendor contracts, or consolidated payroll allocations during an appeal for earlier years, deficiencies in contemporaneous time-tracking and project-code accounting frequently surface, exposing that foreign subcontracting costs, commercial prototype tooling, or non-specialized administrative labour were improperly pooled into SR&ED expenditure pools across multiple fiscal years.
Funded Research Exclusions, Assistance Clawbacks, and Corporate Status Vulnerabilities

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) and the definitions of "government assistance," "non-government assistance," and "contract payment" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA, a taxpayer's qualified SR&ED expenditures must be reduced by any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, or reimbursement received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received, whether from domestic or foreign entities. Medical technology companies operating in the global health arena routinely collaborate with international research centres, charitable foundations, and public health consortia.

Similarly, corporate financing agreements involving foreign institutional investors or venture capital funds can alter a corporation's ownership structure, potentially disqualifying it as a "Canadian-controlled private corporation" (CCPC) under subsection 125(7) and section 256 of the ITA, thereby reducing its ITC rate from the enhanced 35% refundable rate to the 15% non-refundable rate. When a taxpayer voluntarily discloses multi-year corporate minute books, shareholder agreements, or consortium funding contracts during an appeal for 2007–2008, CRA auditors routinely extract clauses showing multi-year grant entitlements, milestone reimbursements, or de facto control shifts that apply to subsequent taxation years, triggering devastating collateral reassessments.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each procedural, statutory, and evidentiary requirement implicated in Fio Corporation v. The Queen (2014 TCC 58) and its broader SR&ED litigation framework against the specific party failures and the governing standard of proof applied by the Canadian courts.

headers: Court's Standard of Proof & Judicial Holding

cells: Applicability of the Implied Undertaking Rule to the Crown
Common Law (Juman v. Doucette, 2008 SCC 8); General Procedure Rules.

Minister's Failure: The Minister argued she is not a "normal litigant" due to her statutory mandate under the ITA and claimed that the implied undertaking rule did not apply where she used discovery information to reassess the same taxpayer for the same issue and taxation year.
Absolute Equality of Litigants: The Tax Court held (paras. 48, 50) that no party receives more favourable treatment before the Court; the Minister is fully bound by the implied undertaking rule.
Interaction Between Section 241 of the ITA and Discovery Rules
ITA, s. 241; Common Law Implied Undertaking Doctrine.
Minister's Failure: The Minister asserted that s. 241 of the ITA is a "complete code" governing taxpayer information that overrides common law discovery restrictions.

No Statutory Override: Section 241 governs administrative confidentiality and its subsection 241(4) merely provides exceptions to the prohibition in subsection 241(1) and does not override common law rules such as the implied undertaking rule (para. 58, comments the Court described as not needed for its decision).
Requirement for Leave of the Court to Vary an Undertaking
Juman v. Doucette, 2008 SCC 8 (paras. 30–34); Fio Corporation v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 58.

Minister's Failure: The Minister unilaterally used disclosed appeal documents to reassess the same 2007 and 2008 taxation years under appeal (with a consequential 2009 adjustment) without applying to the Court for leave.

Balance of Interests Test on Motion: A party seeking collateral use must apply to the Court for leave before using the information (paras. 53–54) and demonstrate a superior public interest in disclosure; leave is never granted automatically, and an undertaking should be set aside only in exceptional circumstances (para. 56, citing Juman).
Compulsion Prerequisite for Attachment of Implied Undertaking
Canada v. Fio Corporation, 2015 FCA 236 (paras. 14–16, 21–22, 24); General Procedure Rules, Rules 81, 82, 95.

Taxpayer's Failure: Fio Corporation sought to rely on the implied undertaking for documents that, on its own affiant's evidence, had already been made available to CRA auditors in 2009 and 2010, before its appeal commenced; it delivered them again under Rule 81 with its Notice of Appeal and a settlement cover letter.

Strict Legal Compulsion Standard: While the implied undertaking applies in the Tax Court, it does not apply to evidence disclosed before the Tax Court proceedings commenced or to evidence a party was not compelled to produce; because the Discovery Documents had been made available to the CRA in 2009 and 2010, the rule did not apply, and the FCA left open whether Rule 81 productions are compelled.
Tax Court Jurisdiction to Remedy Abuse of Process
Tax Court of Canada Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. T-2, ss. 12, 13; ITA s. 171; R. v. Cunningham, 2010 SCC 10; General Procedure Rules, Rule 4.

Minister's Failure: The Minister used the Discovery Documents to reassess without leave of the Court, which the Tax Court found to be an abuse of process that was not inadvertent (paras. 77–79); the reasons do not record the Minister contesting the Court's jurisdiction to vacate an assessment.

Implied Jurisdiction by Necessary Implication: As both a superior court and a statutory court, the Tax Court held that it has implied jurisdiction (applying Cunningham) to control its process and remedy a breach of an undertaking to the Court, including by vacating an assessment where appropriate (para. 71); it declined to vacate, prohibited use of the documents, and awarded substantial (not solicitor-and-client) costs, an order later set aside by 2015 FCA 236 ($25,000 awarded in 2014 TCC 58).
Protective & Confidentiality Orders for Pre-Discovery / Sensitive Data
General Procedure Rules, Rule 4; Sierra Club of Canada, 2002 SCC 41; AB Hassle, 1998 CanLII 8942.

Taxpayer's Failure: (Not addressed in either decision.) Fio Corporation's cover letter sought only an early settlement meeting and contained no confidentiality reservation, and no formal Protective Order was obtained before sharing multi-year proprietary R&D records.

Three-Part Protective Order Standard: The applicant must demonstrate that (i) the information was treated at all times as confidential; (ii) it is intrinsically confidential; and (iii) disclosure could reasonably harm proprietary, commercial, or scientific interests.
Substantive SR&ED Eligibility & Multi-Year Cost Segregation
ITA ss. 37(1), 127(9), 248(1) ("SR&ED"); Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd., [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520.
Taxpayer's Evidentiary Vulnerability: Submitting unsegregated multi-year technical, clinical, and funding records that expose subsequent years to routine-engineering or assistance clawbacks.

Contemporaneous, Fiscal-Year-Specific Proof: The taxpayer bears the burden of proving technological uncertainty, systematic investigation, and unassisted qualified expenditures strictly within each discrete taxation year under appeal.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the legal and procedural holdings of Fio Corporation v. The Queen (2014 TCC 58) and Canada v. Fio Corporation (2015 FCA 236) into actionable compliance and litigation strategy, the following two industry case studies examine realistic Canadian taxpayers confronting the exact procedural and substantive pitfalls identified in the jurisprudence. Each case study provides a step-by-step remedial architecture covering litigation discovery governance, contemporaneous technical documentation, contractual structuring, and systematic experimentation tracking.
Case Study 1: Point-of-Care Biosensor and Mobile Medical Diagnostics Developer (Biotechnology and MedTech Sector)
Project Fact Pattern and Exposure to the Fio Corporation Pitfalls

Vanguard BioDiagnostics Inc. (Vanguard) is an Ontario-based Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) developing an integrated handheld microfluidic biosensor and automated optical reader designed to detect vector-borne pathogen DNA from whole-blood samples in remote clinical settings. Across its 2022, 2023, and 2024 fiscal years (ending December 31), Vanguard claimed $1.8 million per year in qualified SR&ED expenditures and $630,000 per year in refundable 35% ITCs under sections 37 and 127 of the ITA.

Following an audit of the 2022 taxation year, the CRA disallowed 100% of the claim, asserting that Vanguard merely integrated off-the-shelf optical CMOS sensors with standard mobile computing components. After the CRA Appeals Division confirmed the 2022 reassessment, Vanguard filed a Notice of Appeal in the Tax Court of Canada under the General Procedure. Eager to unlock its frozen cash flow and settle the 2022 appeal quickly, Vanguard's Chief Financial Officer proposes sending a comprehensive "Settlement Binder" directly to the Department of Justice counsel alongside the Notice of Appeal, accompanied by a cover letter stating the binder is provided "For Settlement Purposes Only".

An internal pre-litigation legal and technical review of the proposed Settlement Binder reveals four acute exposures mirroring Fio Corporation. First, on a procedural level, because the Settlement Binder would be delivered voluntarily prior to the close of pleadings and outside formal Rule 81 or Rule 82 documentary discovery, the common law implied undertaking rule is unlikely to attach, given the holding in Canada v. Fio Corporation, 2015 FCA 236 (para. 16), that the rule does not apply to evidence a party was not compelled to produce, allowing the CRA to legally forward the binder to its audit division to reassess Vanguard's currently un-audited 2023 and 2024 taxation years. Second, regarding technical spillover, the binder contains a 2024 clinical field evaluation manuscript from a tropical disease study in South America showing that Vanguard's prototype achieved 99.2% diagnostic concordance in late 2022. Disclosing this document without technical demarcation will prompt the CRA to reassess 2023 and 2024 on the ground that all core technological uncertainties were resolved in 2022, rendering the 2023–2024 activities ineligible commercial field validation. Third, regarding contractual assistance, the binder includes an unredacted 2023–2024 Master Collaboration Agreement with an international tropical disease foundation providing $1.2 million in field-testing reimbursements, which the CRA will seize upon to reduce Vanguard's 2023 and 2024 qualified SR&ED expenditure pools as "non-government assistance" or "contract payments" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Fourth, regarding financial costing, the binder includes consolidated multi-year payroll spreadsheets that commingle domestic laboratory biochemical engineering with ineligible foreign clinical trial supervision in South America exceeding the 10% limit under subsection 37(1.5) of the ITA.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Restructuring Litigation and Project Governance to Trigger the Implied Undertaking Shield

Vanguard must immediately halt all voluntary, pre-discovery document transmissions to the Minister or the AGC. Under the combined ratio of 2014 TCC 58 and 2015 FCA 236, corporate tax governance requires establishing a strict litigation discovery firewall. Counsel for Vanguard must file the Notice of Appeal containing strictly pleaded material facts pursuant to Rule 48 without attaching evidentiary exhibits or delivering accompanying settlement binders. Vanguard must wait until the Respondent files the Reply to the Notice of Appeal under Rule 49 and the Court issues a formal timetable order governing documentary discovery.

To maximize the likelihood that the common law implied undertaking rule recognized in 2014 TCC 58 and Juman v. Doucette, 2008 SCC 8, attaches (bearing in mind that it never covers documents already provided to the CRA, for example during the audit, and that the Federal Court of Appeal in 2015 FCA 236 left open whether Rule 81 productions are compelled), all supporting documents should be disclosed only within the Court's discovery process, by way of a List of Documents served under Rule 81 (partial disclosure) or Rule 82 (full disclosure) of the General Procedure Rules, or in response to formal undertakings given during an Examination for Discovery under Rule 95. Where the rule attaches, 2014 TCC 58 indicates that the Minister must apply to the Tax Court for leave before using those documents to reassess the 2023 or 2024 taxation years, although the Federal Court of Appeal observed that the Department of Justice may properly send to the CRA documents that had previously been made available to CRA auditors. Furthermore, for highly sensitive multi-year scientific data—such as proprietary DNA primer sequences and biosensor calibration algorithms—Vanguard should apply to the Tax Court under Rule 4 for a formal Protective and Confidentiality Order prior to inspection, satisfying the three-part test applied by the Tax Court by demonstrating that the information has been treated at all relevant times as confidential, is intrinsically confidential, and that disclosure could reasonably harm Vanguard's proprietary, commercial, and scientific interests. The order must explicitly stipulate that documents produced in the 2022 docket cannot be accessed by CRA audit personnel assigned to subsequent fiscal years. Simultaneously, every document included in the 2022 List of Documents must undergo a rigorous fiscal-year redaction protocol, whereby any data columns, project milestones, or financial ledger entries pertaining to the 2023 and 2024 taxation years that are not relevant to the issues pleaded in the 2022 appeal are redacted on grounds of irrelevance prior to production, preventing inadvertent multi-year audit spillover.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation to Isolate Year-Over-Year Technological Uncertainty

To prevent the CRA from using 2022 technical disclosures to invalidate the 2023 and 2024 SR&ED claims, Vanguard must restructure its technical documentation architecture to establish distinct, non-overlapping technological uncertainties for each fiscal year in accordance with Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. Technical records for the 2022 fiscal year must be framed strictly around the system-level uncertainty of achieving uniform capillary flow and optical fluorescence excitation within a disposable microfluidic cartridge using whole unlysed blood. The 2022 Project Closure Report must document that while static benchtop optical reading succeeded in December 2022, severe technological uncertainties emerged when exposing the biosensor to high-humidity, high-temperature tropical ambient environments (up to 40°C and 90% relative humidity).

Rather than characterizing the 2023–2024 activities as clinical field validation of the 2022 reader, Vanguard must establish a new, distinct SR&ED project for 2023–2024 focusing on thermal-stable reagent lyophilization and automated machine-vision compensation for degraded rapid diagnostic assays. The contemporaneous engineering logs must prove that the 2023 field data from South America was not commercial validation, but rather experimental baseline data revealing unexpected reagent degradation and non-linear optical scatter, which required formulating new biochemical and algorithmic hypotheses in Canada throughout 2023 and 2024.
Step 3: Restructuring Contractual Terms to Prevent Assistance Clawbacks

To neutralize the risk that Vanguard's collaboration with the international tropical disease foundation will be reassessed as "non-government assistance" or a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, Vanguard must bifurcate its Master Collaboration Agreement into two legally distinct instruments. The first instrument should be a Commercial Device Supply and Field Logistics Agreement governing the sale of physical prototype cartridges and foreign clinical site administration in South America, none of which is claimed for Canadian SR&ED. The second instrument should govern an Unfunded Domestic Core IP Research Program conducted solely in Ontario, for which Vanguard receives zero reimbursements, grants, or subsidies from the foundation. By contractually tying 100% of the foundation's funding to the non-SR&ED foreign clinical site administration and commercial device supply deliverables, Vanguard ensures that no portion of the funding can be characterized as an amount received "in respect of" the domestic SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(d) or subsection 127(9) of the ITA.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation Tracking and Financial Costing

Vanguard must overhaul its internal accounting and experimentation tracking systems to establish an impenetrable audit trail. Every experimental iteration conducted in Ontario must be logged in an immutable electronic laboratory notebook (ELN) and code repository tagged with a fiscal-year-specific Hypothesis ID, recording the quantitative baseline metric, the technological bottleneck, the experimental variable manipulated, the empirical test data, and the analytical conclusion. In parallel, Vanguard must implement automated time-tracking and general ledger sub-accounts that strictly segregate domestic SR&ED experimentation under subsection 37(1) from foreign clinical trial support under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), ensuring that any payroll spreadsheet produced in litigation is already cleanly partitioned by statutory category and taxation year.
Case Study 2: Industrial Low-Speed Telemetry and Embedded RF Hardware Manufacturer (Advanced Electronics and Telecommunications Sector)
Project Fact Pattern and Exposure to the Fio Corporation Pitfalls

Apex Telemetry Systems Corp. (Apex) is a British Columbia-based designer and manufacturer of industrial low-speed multipoint digital radio transceivers and embedded electromagnetic sensors used in high-interference automated mining and automotive environments. Across its 2023 and 2024 taxation years, Apex claimed $2.4 million in SR&ED expenditures for developing a next-generation ultra-low-power transceiver operating in uncoordinated frequency bands while attempting to suppress voltage fluctuations, flicker, and specific absorption rate (SAR) electromagnetic emissions.

During the CRA's audit of the 2023 taxation year, the CRA Research and Technology Advisor requested copies of Apex's electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) test failures. Apex declined to provide certain internal engineering post-mortems during the audit, leading the CRA to deny the 2023 claim for lack of documentary evidence. Apex filed a Notice of Objection and subsequently a Notice of Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.

During the litigation of the 2023 appeal, Apex produced 4,000 pages of internal engineering logs, multi-year customer supply contracts with an international automotive Tier-1 supplier, and EMC testing records under its Rule 81 List of Documents. Upon reviewing Apex's Rule 81 discovery production, the Department of Justice counsel noticed that several engineering logs dated in 2024 showed that Apex's engineers had been paid milestone fees by the Tier-1 automotive customer for passing international type-approval standards, specifically ETSI EN 301 489-1 and CISPR 11. Without seeking leave from the Tax Court of Canada, the Department of Justice counsel emailed the 2024 discovery documents to a CRA audit team leader in Vancouver, who immediately opened an audit and issued a Notice of Reassessment denying Apex's 2024 SR&ED claim and assessing penalties.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Enforcing the Implied Undertaking Rule via an Interlocutory Sanction Motion

Unlike Case Study 1—where the taxpayer disclosed documents voluntarily prior to discovery—Apex disclosed its 4,000 pages of documents as part of Rule 81 documentary discovery after the close of pleadings. Consequently, Apex has a strong argument, grounded in the reasoning of Fio Corporation v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 58 (paras. 39 and 60–62), that the common law implied undertaking rule attached when Apex produced those documents in discovery, particularly because many of its engineering post-mortems were withheld during the audit and first disclosed in the appeal, unlike Fio, where all of the documents had been made available to CRA auditors before the appeal (2015 FCA 236, paras. 21–22); however, 2014 TCC 58 was set aside on appeal, and the Federal Court of Appeal expressly left open whether Rule 81 productions are compelled (para. 24).

Counsel for Apex must immediately bring an interlocutory motion before the Tax Court citing Fio Corporation v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 58, and Juman v. Doucette, 2008 SCC 8. The motion record must establish through affidavit evidence and cross-examination on affidavits that the CRA auditor relied on documents bearing Apex's Rule 81 discovery Bates-numbers from the 2023 appeal to issue the 2024 reassessment, and that the Minister never applied to the Tax Court for an order varying the implied undertaking prior to that collateral use. Should the Crown argue that subsection 241(4) of the ITA permitted the Department of Justice to share the documents with CRA auditors for the administration and enforcement of the ITA, Apex will rely, as persuasive authority, on paragraphs 48, 50 and 58 of 2014 TCC 58 to establish that the Minister is not above the law, receives no special treatment as a litigant, and cannot invoke section 241 to override the common law implied undertaking owed to the Tax Court. Relying on the jurisdictional holdings in 2014 TCC 58, Apex should request that the Court exercise its implied jurisdiction to control its process by issuing an evidentiary prohibition order barring the Minister from using any of the 2023 discovery documents or derivative information in the 2024 reassessment proceeding, ordering the quarantine and destruction of the improperly transferred discovery files within the CRA's 2024 audit file, vacating the 2024 reassessment if the Minister cannot sustain the reassessment independently of the tainted discovery documents, and awarding elevated lump-sum costs patterned on the $25,000 costs award in 2014 TCC 58 (an award set aside, with the rest of that order, by 2015 FCA 236), payable forthwith by the Minister.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation to Separate Regulatory Type-Approval from Experimental RF Design

Even after purging the tainted discovery documents from the 2024 audit, Apex must ensure its underlying 2024 technical documentation can withstand an independent, untainted CRA audit. In the telecommunications and electronics industry, the CRA routinely disallows work related to international regulatory standards such as ETSI, CENELEC, and CISPR electromagnetic compatibility certifications, characterizing such testing as routine quality assurance or commercial certification excluded under paragraph (f) or (i) of the subsection 248(1) SR&ED definition.

Apex must restructure its technical narratives so that standards like CISPR 11 or EN 50364 are never described as the objective of the project. Instead, the technical documentation must articulate a fundamental physical conflict in radio frequency engineering: achieving reliable multipoint digital packet transmission at 10 mW power output in high-noise industrial environments without inducing harmonic impedance mismatches that degrade signal integrity below −110 dBm sensitivity. Standard pass/fail certification tests conducted at third-party accredited compliance laboratories must be excluded from the SR&ED claim, whereas internal anechoic chamber tests where engineers systematically alter printed circuit board ground-plane geometries, metamaterial shielding structures, and active phase-cancellation firmware to test hypotheses regarding electromagnetic field attenuation must be documented in dedicated SR&ED Experimental Logs.
Step 3: Restructuring Customer Co-Development Contracts to Avoid the Contract Payment Trap

Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, an amount paid or payable to Apex by a "taxable supplier" (a person resident in Canada, a Canadian partnership, or a non-resident paying in the course of carrying on business through a permanent establishment in Canada) for SR&ED performed "for or on behalf of" an arm's-length customer entitled to a deduction under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) or (i.1) is a "contract payment", which under subsection 127(18) reduces the qualified SR&ED expenditures on which Apex can claim ITCs. Apex must amend its supply agreements with the Tier-1 automotive customer to explicitly state that the customer is contracting solely for the purchase of commercial production units or pre-production commercial samples at a fixed unit price, contingent upon those units meeting commercial specifications. The contract must expressly stipulate that Apex is not being engaged to perform SR&ED on behalf of the customer, that Apex retains 100% legal and beneficial ownership of all background and foreground intellectual property, schematics, and firmware developed, and that any non-recurring engineering (NRE) or milestone payments are strictly refundable commercial deposits against future unit deliveries rather than reimbursements for R&D labour.
Step 4: Implementing Granular Experimentation and Cost-Tracking Controls

To prevent future documentary commingling during either administrative audits or Tax Court discovery, Apex must configure its Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) and engineering ticket systems with mandatory Work-Breakdown Structure (WBS) gates that separate experimental radio frequency architecture and hypothesis testing (eligible SR&ED) from type-approval certification and customer sample qualification (non-SR&ED commercial engineering). Every technical document, test log, and financial voucher must be indexed at creation by taxation year, project code, and WBS phase. In the event of a Tax Court appeal for a single taxation year, Apex can generate a strictly scoped Rule 81 or Rule 82 List of Documents containing solely the records relevant to that specific fiscal year, helping ensure that disclosed documents not previously provided to the CRA fall within the implied undertaking rule applied in Fio Corporation v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 58, while eliminating any extraneous multi-year disclosures.
5. Synthesis and Strategic Recommendations for Canadian Tax Practitioners

The litigation trajectory of Fio Corporation v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 58, and Canada v. Fio Corporation, 2015 FCA 236, delivers an enduring lesson for Canadian SR&ED tax counsel, corporate controllers, and R&D directors. While the Tax Court of Canada in 2014 TCC 58 insisted on the equality of litigants and sanctioned the Minister with substantial costs and an evidentiary prohibition for using discovery documents to reassess without leave, an order the Federal Court of Appeal set aside in 2015 FCA 236, the protection of the implied undertaking rule is strictly contingent on the documents not having been disclosed to the CRA before the appeal and on their production being compelled in the litigation. By channeling all litigation disclosures through the formal discovery processes of Rules 81, 82, and 95 of the General Procedure Rules, securing pre-production Protective Orders under Rule 4 where proprietary multi-year science is at stake, and maintaining rigorous fiscal-year boundaries across technical narratives, commercial contracts, and accounting ledgers, Canadian claimants can robustly defend their SR&ED tax credits without exposing adjacent taxation years to collateral audit risk.
